intrinsic_value_estimate: About $94–112 per share in the base case. Method: 1987 owner earnings of $2.04–2.43/share (reported earnings excluding one-time items, plus depreciation and amortization, less capex; capex taken either as total capex or as equal to depreciation), grown at 12% for 10 years in line with the 11–13% EPS record, then 5%, discounted at an assumed ~9% long bond rate (the rate is not in the packet). Sensitivities: growth cut to 8% gives $68–81; management's 12% cost of capital gives $51–61; 8% growth at 12% gives $38–45 (the downside case). Net working capital test: about $0.05/share, a fail, but not the governing test for this kind of business.
margin_of_safety: Price of $46.56 is 42–50% of base-case value, a margin of about 50–58%. With growth cut to 8%, the margin is still about 32–43%. At management's 12% hurdle it is about 9–24%. The margin turns negative only if slow growth and a 12% required return occur together. The framework sets no numeric hurdle for an outstanding business, only that the price must 'make sense even should the future … develop much along the lines of its past' (brk-letter-1981#3), and that is met with room to spare. The protection comes mainly from the predictability of the franchise, not from a balance-sheet discount.

key_reasons.reason: This is a high-return business without needing leverage: return on equity has been about 19–29% for more than a decade, and the core business earns far more than that on its own capital.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §3 Return on equity, not EPS growth, is the primary test (brk-letter-1979)
key_reasons.evidence: ROE: 20.6% (1977), 19.9% (1981), 27.2% (1987). In 1987 soft-drink operating income was $1,433M on $4.17B of identifiable assets (about 34% pretax), and International earned $1,109M on $2,127M (about 52%). Debt/capital was 3.5–9% through 1981. Net debt/capital is 15.3% at end-1987 (ar-1987).

key_reasons.reason: There is a wide and widening moat built on brand, distribution scale and pricing power, and it has proven durable even through management's own mistake.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §3 Durable competitive advantage: the moat around the castle (brk-letter-1986#16)
key_reasons.evidence: World's best-known trademark; about 44% of world soft-drink volume, double the nearest competitor; US fountain share 59%, more than 2-to-1 over the nearest rival; about 63% gross margin on US concentrate; contracts allow price changes 'at its discretion'; 1987 US cola lead the 'widest gap in more than 10 years'; Coca-Cola classic became the #1 US soft drink after the 1985 formula change (ar-1986, ar-1987).

key_reasons.reason: Owner earnings are high relative to reported earnings because the core business needs little reinvestment just to stand still, and there is a long runway for growth.
key_reasons.evidence: 1987: net income $916M + D&A $153.5M − capex $299.6M = about $770M ($2.04/share) treating all capex as required, up to $2.43 if maintenance capex equals depreciation. Soft-drink capex of $170M is about 12% of soft-drink operating income. International per-capita consumption is 16% of the US level (ar-1986, ar-1987).

key_reasons.reason: Retained earnings have produced far more than $1 of market value per $1 retained during this management team's tenure.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §4 Each $1 retained must create at least $1 of market value (brk-letter-1983)
key_reasons.evidence: From end-1981 to end-1987: $5.18/share retained ($10.97 EPS − $5.79 dividends) against a price rise from $11.58 to $38.13 (now $46.56) on about the same 372M shares. Even excluding the P/E re-rating, about $2 of value was created per $1 retained.

key_reasons.reason: An able management team is in place and has refocused on the core business with an explicit cost-of-capital discipline, reversing most of its diversification mistakes.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §4 Honest, able management already in place; candid reporting (brk-letter-1979, brk-letter-1982)
key_reasons.evidence: Goizueta/Keough since 1981; Entertainment spun into 49%-owned CPE via a $335M in-kind dividend; 51% of CCE and TCC sold to the public; soft drinks are 'more than 95 percent of operating income'; 12% after-tax hurdle stated; 'preferring investments within our existing lines of business' (ar-1987).

key_reasons.reason: The price makes sense if the future resembles the past: a good business at a sensible price, not a bargain-bin purchase.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §5 Valuation as of this date: 'outstanding business at a sensible price, not a mediocre business at a bargain price' (brk-letter-1987#18); 'prices that will make sense, even should the future … develop much along the lines of its past' (brk-letter-1981#3). The net-working-capital rule (bpl-letter-1965) is noted and failed.
key_reasons.evidence: $46.56 = 19.2x 1987 EPS of $2.43; owner-earnings yield 4.4–5.2%, which grows to about 14–16% on cost after 10 years at the historical 12% growth rate; base-case value $94–112 (prices; Stage 4).

key_reasons.reason: No catalyst is needed, and the recent price rise is not a reason to wait or to buy.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §6 No catalyst needed: the market eventually reflects business results; §9 No market forecasting (brk-letter-1987, bpl-letter-1966-mid)
key_reasons.evidence: Stock near the top of its 52-week range ($35.04–49.12); company buying back up to 40M shares (more than 10% of shares) by 1990, which increases each remaining share's claim on the business (ar-1987, prices).

key_reasons.reason: A concentrated position is justified because the chance of anything drastically changing the underlying value is very low. It is held below the 40% maximum because several facts are missing from the packet.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §7 Concentrate when the facts are clear: up to 40% (bpl-letter-1965)
key_reasons.evidence: A century-old product, an unbroken earnings record, simple economics; but the packet lacks 1988 results, the discount rate and the maintenance capex split, and gives no first-hand view of management.

key_reasons.reason: The size fits Berkshire's elephant-hunting criterion: a large position is possible in a liquid stock.
key_reasons.evidence: Market value about $17.3B; net income $916M vs the $10M minimum; a stake of about $0.75B (25% of an assumed ~$3B of Berkshire capital) would be only about 4% of the company (prices; Berkshire capital assumed).

risks: 1988 results are not in the packet; the valuation rests on 1987 figures and the assumption that the trend continued.
Currency: about 77% of soft-drink operating income is earned abroad, and the 1986–87 gains were helped by key currencies rising 27% and 16%. A stronger dollar would reverse part of this.
Value is sensitive to the discount rate: at management's 12% combined with 8% growth, the price (about $38–45 value) is near or above value.

Leverage policy: gross debt/capital rose to 45.6% (target of 35% on a net basis) to fund buybacks; contingent guarantees of about $394M, receivables sold with recourse, and an unconsolidated finance subsidiary adding about $300M of debt.
Capital allocation: about $2.3B sits in bottling and film affiliates earning about 5%. There is a history of issuing stock for Columbia and Embassy, and management could diversify again.
Buybacks are justified by 'excess cash and debt capacity' rather than by price against intrinsic value.
Volume is price-sensitive (Germany −4% after price rises); Latin America has low margins and hyperinflation; heavy ongoing advertising is needed ($720M of media spending in 1987).
Foods business is in decline and restructuring ($36M charge, management change).
The reports are promotional; repeated 'one-time' provisions and restatements make the reported earnings harder to read.
what_would_change_my_mind: 1988 results showing soft-drink volume or profit growth stalling in local currency (i.e., excluding currency gains), or a sustained loss of US or fountain share.
Evidence that a large part of capex is maintenance rather than growth, pushing owner earnings well below about $2.00/share.
Management resuming major acquisitions outside the soft-drink business, especially if paid for in stock (brk-letter-1982#17).
Leverage rising above the 35% net target, or buybacks continuing at prices clearly above a conservative estimate of intrinsic value.
Long-term interest rates rising enough to make the 12%-rate cases the relevant ones, removing the margin of safety.
First-hand evidence (meetings, proxy statement) that management's integrity or attitude toward owners falls short of the standard applied to the permanent holdings.
A price rise that pushes the stock well above base-case value before the position is built; this would slow or stop further buying, though not existing ownership.
sell_triggers: The franchise economics turn out to have been misread: a lasting loss of pricing power, or concentrate returns falling toward those of an ordinary business ('far easier to exit from' a marketable security, brk-letter-1987#18).
Management repeatedly destroys value through share-issuing diversification or by retaining earnings that fail the $1-for-$1 test over a reasonable period (brk-letter-1983).
Management shows a lack of candor or integrity that undermines trust in the reported numbers.
Not a trigger: the stock price rising or the P/E expanding. The default for a great business with able managers is to hold permanently (§8, brk-letter-1987#18).
